content: Dental sealants are a preventive dental treatment that involves the application of a plastic material to one or more teeth. The primary purpose of this treatment is to prevent dental caries (commonly known as cavities) and other forms of tooth decay. Since the 1970s in the United States, the prevalence of tooth decay on the smooth surfaces of teeth has decreased. This decline is partly attributed to the widespread fluoridation of public water supplies and improved dental hygiene practices among the general population. However, the molars and premolars located at the back of the mouth have complex biting surfaces with numerous pits and fissures. These areas are often challenging to clean thoroughly, even with diligent tooth-brushing efforts. To address this issue, research into dental sealants began in the 1960s, and by the early 1970s, the first generation of sealants was developed and approved by the FDA. Dental sealants are typically applied in a dental office. The procedure begins with the dentist or dental assistant cleaning and drying the tooth that will be treated. A thin layer of liquid plastic material is then painted onto the pits and fissures of the tooth. Once the plastic material is applied, a blue-spectrum natural light is used to cure the material, hardening it within seconds. Alternatively, some brands of sealants are designed to self-cure through a chemical process. After curing, the plastic forms a hard, thin layer that covers the treated areas of the tooth. Despite the significant forces exerted on teeth during daily chewing, dental sealants can remain effective for five years or longer. However, they naturally wear down over time and may become damaged. In some cases, bacteria and food particles can become trapped beneath the sealants, potentially leading to decay in the very teeth the sealants were intended to protect.
